alignment.note: δέ / ܕܝܢ / autem — postpositive connective preserved across all three.

Greek ἤδη ('already') is matched by the Vulgate jam, but the Peshitta omits the temporal adverb entirely, conflating it into the conditional clause introduced by ܕܡܐ ܕܪܟ. This is a typical Syriac economy of temporal modifiers rather than a substantive textual variant.

The verb of the Greek clause (γένηται 'becomes tender') is rendered by the Peshitta with the verb ܕܪܟ ('grows/becomes soft') placed before its subject ܣܘܟܝܗ ('its branch'), whereas Greek and Latin keep subject (ὁ κλάδος αὐτῆς / ramus ejus) before the predicate. The Syriac fuses the predicate ἁπαλὸς γένηται into a single verb.

Greek expresses 'becomes tender' analytically with adjective ἁπαλός plus copula-like γένηται, mirrored by the Vulgate tener fuerit; the Peshitta collapses both into the single finite verb ܕܪܟ, a synthetic construction conveying the same maturation idea.

Greek ἐκφύῃ ('puts forth, sprouts') is rendered in the Peshitta by ܦܪܥܘ (root p-r-ʿ, 'to sprout/bring forth shoots'), a precise botanical cognate; the Vulgate uses the passive periphrasis nata fuerint ('have been born/produced'), shifting agency from the branch to the leaves themselves.

Greek γινώσκετε and Latin cognoscitis carry the 2nd-person plural within the verb form, whereas the Peshitta makes the subject explicit with the participle ܝܕܥܝܢ plus the independent pronoun ܐܢܬܘܢ ('you know'), the standard Syriac enclitic-pronoun construction for the present tense.

Greek and Latin both use a copular construction (ἐγγὺς...ἐστίν / in proximo sit) with the noun 'summer' (θέρος / æstas) as subject; the Peshitta employs the verb ܡܛܐ ('has arrived/drawn near') governing ܩܝܛܐ ('summer'), turning the adverbial predicate of nearness into a finite verb of arrival — semantically equivalent but syntactically distinct.

The Clementine Vulgate closes the verse with a colon, marking continuation into the following apodosis; neither the Greek full stop nor the Peshitta's unpunctuated text shares this editorial division.
